pos: n. (proper name; one of the twelve apostles, also called Lebbaeus and Judas the brother of James)
etymology: Greek Thaddaios, probably from an Aramaic root signifying the breast, hence a warm or large-hearted man; one of the twelve.
biblical_def: Thaddaeus is an apostle of Jesus Christ, named among the twelve in two of the lists and absent by that name from the other two. The calling is given first: “And when he had called unto him his twelve disciples, he gave them power against unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease” (Matthew 10:1). Matthew's roll then gives him two names at once: “Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus” (Matthew 10:3). Mark lists him simply: “And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Canaanite” (Mark 3:18). Luke, in the gospel and in the Acts, calls the same man Judas the brother of James: “where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James” (Acts 1:13). So one apostle is remembered under three names, and not one word he spoke is recorded in the gospels except a single question at the Supper. He held an office equal to Peter's and left no sermon. The Lord's work does not require that every servant be quoted.

corruption_summary: Usefulness is measured by visibility; an apostle of Christ left no recorded sermon and lost nothing of his office.
corruption_paragraphs: A ministry is now weighed by its platform, and a man with no quotable output is assumed to have contributed little. Thaddaeus held the apostolic office, received power against unclean spirits, and was sent out with the twelve. Scripture preserves hardly a syllable from him. The office was real and the obscurity was real at the same time.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faithfulness in an appointed place is the measure of a servant, and that God is free to leave a true minister almost unrecorded.

pos: n. (one of the nomadic peoples north of the Black Sea; a byword in antiquity for savagery)
etymology: Greek Skuthes, a Scythian, from the nomadic nations of the steppe north of the Euxine sea; used once in Scripture, at Colossians 3:11.
biblical_def: Scythian occurs once in the whole Bible, and it is placed where it does the most work. Paul has told the Colossians to put off the old man: “Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds” (Colossians 3:9), and to put on the new: “And have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him” (Colossians 3:10). Then he names the company into which the new man is put: “Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all” (Colossians 3:11). To a Greek ear Scythian was the last word in that list by design. The Scythians of the northern steppe were, in the common speech of the ancient world, the most savage of the barbarians — the people one named when one meant beyond civilising. Paul puts the Scythian in the church. The parallel in Galatians draws the same circle: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). Oneness in Christ does not abolish the distinctions it names; it abolishes their power to divide those whom Christ has joined.

corruption_summary: Colossians 3:11 is read as the erasure of all distinction; Paul names the distinctions and denies them the power to divide the body.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is now commonly cited to prove that in Christ the categories of nation, station and sex are abolished as such — that to be in Christ is to be nothing in particular. But Paul keeps naming them in the same breath that he unites them: Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, Barbarian and Scythian, bond and free. He is not flattening the creation; he is telling a Greek that the Scythian is his brother and that neither of them is the church's foundation, for Christ is all, and in all.

The honest force of the verse is harder than its popular use. The Scythian was the man a cultured Colossian would have despised on sight, and he is seated at the table. A congregation that quotes this text while keeping its own despised classes outside has not understood it.

pos: n. (a woman of the Jewish nation)
etymology: English, the feminine of Jew, from Hebrew Yehudi, a man of Judah; used by the Authorized Version at Acts 16:1 and Acts 24:24.
biblical_def: Jewess is the Authorized Version's word for a woman of the Jewish nation, and it is used of two women who could hardly be less alike. The first is the mother of Timothy: “Then came he to Derbe and Lystra: and, behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus, the son of a certain woman, which was a Jewess, and believed; but his father was a Greek” (Acts 16:1). She was in a mixed marriage, she believed, and she had taught her son the Scriptures from a child. The brethren had taken note of the young man: “Which was well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium” (Acts 16:2), and Paul took him along, circumcising him for the sake of the Jews of those quarters: “Him would Paul have to go forth with him; and took and circumcised him because of the Jews which were in those quarters” (Acts 16:3). The second Jewess in Scripture is Drusilla, a daughter of the house of Herod, sitting beside the governor who kept Paul in bonds for two years: “And after certain days, when Felix came with his wife Drusilla, which was a Jewess, he sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ” (Acts 24:24). One Jewish mother raised a minister of the gospel; one Jewish princess heard the gospel and went back to her husband's court. Blood was the same in both; the issue was faith.

corruption_paragraphs: Scripture is read in our time through the grid of identity, so that a woman's standing before God is assumed to follow from her people. Acts uses the one word of a believing mother in a mixed household and of a Herodian princess who heard Paul preach and was unmoved. The same descent, two different ends. Grace is not inherited.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is that a godly mother's teaching of the Scriptures to her child is a work of the first order, and that hearing the faith of Christ at one's ease is no substitute for believing it.

pos: n. (Judea; the land of the Jews)
etymology: Middle English Jewerie, the quarter or country of the Jews, from Jew, Hebrew Yehudi; the Authorized Version's older English for Judea.
biblical_def: Jewry is the Authorized Version's older English name for Judea, the land of the Jews. It appears in the mouth of a heathen king: “Then was Daniel brought in before the king. And the king spake and said unto Daniel, Art thou that Daniel, which art of the children of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought out of Jewry?” (Daniel 5:13). Belshazzar locates the prophet by the land his father had emptied. In the Gospels the word names the territory in which our Lord's ministry was most dangerous to Him. His accusers used it before Pilate: “And they were the more fierce, saying, He stirreth up the people, teaching throughout all Jewry, beginning from Galilee to this place” (Luke 23:5). And John uses it to explain a season of His walking in the north: “After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him” (John 7:1). The next verse marks the time: “Now the Jews' feast of tabernacles was at hand” (John 7:2). The word is not a slur in the Authorized Version; it is simply the old English for Judea, as Jewry once named the Jewish quarter of an English town.

corruption_paragraphs: Because the word has been put to ugly uses in later centuries, readers now flinch at it in the Authorized Version and some suspect the translators of malice. The suspicion is unfounded. Jewry is the English of 1611 for Judea, used by a Babylonian king, by Christ's accusers and by the apostle John alike, with no more edge than the word Judea carries today.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the text itself, though the word has been loaded from outside it. The principle to recover is that an old translation must be read in its own English, and that charity, not suspicion, is the first duty of a reader.

pos: n. (one who holds power; in Scripture, a title of God)
etymology: Latin potentatus, dominion or supreme power, from potens, powerful, from posse, to be able; used once in Scripture, at 1 Timothy 6:15.
biblical_def: Potentate is a word for one who holds power, and in Scripture it is used exactly once, of God. Paul has charged Timothy to keep the commandment spotless until the appearing of Christ: “That thou keep this commandment without spot, unrebukeable, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Timothy 6:14). Then he names the one who will set the hour of that appearing: “Which in his times he shall shew, who is the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15). The only is the weight of the verse. Timothy lived under an emperor who was called lord and god; Paul says there is one Potentate and that He is blessed, which no Caesar was. The next verse piles the incommunicable attributes on: “Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom be honour and power everlasting. Amen” (1 Timothy 6:16). The same two titles are written on the thigh of the rider at the end of the Revelation: “And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS” (Revelation 19:16). What Paul gives to God, John sees worn by Christ.

corruption_paragraphs: Every age has its powers that ask to be treated as final — a throne, a party, a court, a market. Paul wrote to a young minister in an empire whose ruler took divine titles, and told him there is one Potentate only. The adjective matters as much as the noun: this one is blessed, happy in Himself, needing nothing from the governments that imitate Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sole, blessed sovereignty of God, who alone has immortality, and who appoints the times in which the Lord Jesus Christ shall appear.

pos: n. (a name given by their enemies to the first Christians)
etymology: Greek Nazoraios, of Nazareth; applied to the followers of Jesus of Nazareth, and used once in the plural, at Acts 24:5.
biblical_def: Nazarenes is the name the enemies of the gospel gave to the first Christians, taking the despised town of their Master and making a party-name of it. The prophecy behind it is noted by Matthew: “And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene” (Matthew 2:23). The plural appears once, in the indictment Tertullus laid before Felix: “For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes” (Acts 24:5). Paul did not refuse the label, but he corrected the charge under it: “But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets” (Acts 24:14), and he named the hope the accusers themselves professed: “And have hope toward God, which they themselves also allow, that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust” (Acts 24:15). He would not be called a sectary, because he held the whole of the law and the prophets; but he was content to be named from the town men used as an insult.

webster_full: Nazarene, an inhabitant of Nazareth, a town of Galilee.

corruption_summary: Christianity is filed as a sect among sects; Paul owned the nickname and denied the category, holding all that the law and prophets wrote.
corruption_paragraphs: The world prefers to classify the faith as one party among many — a sect with its own preferences, to be tolerated so long as it makes no claim on anyone else. Tertullus filed exactly that charge. Paul answered that he worshipped the God of his fathers and believed everything written in the law and in the prophets. A man who believes the whole revelation is not a sectary, whatever his accusers call him.

Believers should expect the nickname and refuse the reduction. Being named from a despised town is no injury; being treated as the holder of a private opinion, when one holds the public truth about God and the resurrection of the dead, is a lie to be corrected plainly, as Paul corrected it before a governor.

pos: v.t. (to bring forward, to exhibit; used of God's challenge to the idols)
etymology: Latin producere, to lead or bring forward, from pro, forward, and ducere, to lead; used once in Scripture, at Isaiah 41:21.
biblical_def: Produce in the Authorized Version is not a noun for garden goods but a verb of the courtroom: to bring a thing forward, to lay the evidence out where it can be examined. It occurs once, and it is God summoning the idols of the nations to trial: “Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong reasons, saith the King of Jacob” (Isaiah 41:21). The test He sets them is prophecy. Let them tell what has been and what shall be: “Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen: let them shew the former things, what they be, that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or declare us things for to come” (Isaiah 41:22). If they can do it, their claim stands: “Shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods: yea, do good, or do evil, that we may be dismayed, and behold it together” (Isaiah 41:23). And the verdict is total silence: “Who hath declared from the beginning, that we may know? and beforetime, that we may say, He is righteous? yea, there is none that sheweth, yea, there is none that declareth, yea, there is none that heareth your words” (Isaiah 41:26). God does not ask the idols for devotion or for sincerity. He asks them for evidence, and they have none.

corruption_paragraphs: It is now commonly held that faith is a private posture which no evidence can establish or overturn, and that it is impolite to ask a religion for proof. Isaiah forty-one is God Himself demanding proof — of the idols, in open court, with the nations watching. The God of Scripture rests His claim on what He has declared beforehand and then brought to pass.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is that the true God stakes His glory on fulfilled prophecy, invites the trial, and that the gods of the nations are convicted by their silence about the future.

pos: n. (proper name; the father of blind Bartimaeus)
etymology: Greek Timaios, probably from time, honour; the name is preserved in that of his son, Bar-Timaeus, son of Timaeus.
biblical_def: Timaeus is named once in Scripture, and only as a father: “And they came to Jericho: and as he went out of Jericho with his disciples and a great number of people, blind Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, sat by the highway side begging” (Mark 10:46). His son's name carries his own — Bar-Timaeus is son of Timaeus — and the son is one of the few men healed by Christ whose name the gospels trouble to record. What that son did at the roadside is the whole reason we know the father's name: “And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, and say, Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me” (Mark 10:47). The crowd rebuked him and he cried louder, and when he was called he came and was asked plainly what he wanted: “And Jesus answered and said unto him, What wilt thou that I should do unto thee? The blind man said unto him, Lord, that I might receive my sight” (Mark 10:51). The answer was given at once: “And Jesus said unto him, Go thy way; thy faith hath made thee whole. And immediately he received his sight, and followed Jesus in the way” (Mark 10:52). A man is remembered in Scripture because his son begged and believed.

corruption_paragraphs: We are taught to measure a life by what a man builds in it. Timaeus built nothing the record notices. He is in the Bible because his blind son would not be silenced, cried after the Son of David, and received his sight. A father may be known for ever by the faith of his child.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ answers the importunate beggar, that He asks a man plainly what he wants, and that sight received is meant to end in following Him in the way.

etymology: From Syria; the Authorized Version's name for the Syrian or Aramaic language, used at Daniel 2:4 at the point where the book itself changes tongue.
biblical_def: Syriack is the Authorized Version's name for the Syrian or Aramaic tongue, and it stands at one of the most remarkable seams in all of Scripture. The book of Daniel opens in Hebrew, and at the moment the Chaldean wise men speak it changes language, and the text itself tells the reader so: “Then spake the Chaldeans to the king in Syriack, O king, live for ever: tell thy servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation” (Daniel 2:4). From that verse to the end of chapter seven the book is written in Aramaic, the common speech of the empires, and then it returns to Hebrew. The chapter shows why the court needed interpreters at all. The king would not tell them the dream: “The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, The thing is gone from me: if ye will not make known unto me the dream, with the interpretation thereof, ye shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill” (Daniel 2:5). They pleaded for the terms of their trade: “They answered again and said, Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation of it” (Daniel 2:7). And at last they confessed their limit in words that condemn their whole profession: “And it is a rare thing that the king requireth, and there is none other that can shew it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh” (Daniel 2:11).

corruption_summary: The change of language in Daniel is treated as evidence against the book; the text itself announces the change at the verse it happens.
corruption_paragraphs: Critics have long used Daniel's two languages as a lever against its unity and its date, as though a book that shifts tongue must be a patchwork. But the shift is not concealed; the narrative names it. The Chaldeans spoke in Syriack, and the record of what the Gentile courts said and saw is given in the Gentile language, while the visions given to Israel return to Hebrew. That is a design, not a seam left by a forger.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is that the wise men of Babylon confessed their own impotence in their own tongue, and that God answered through a captive youth what the gods whose dwelling is not with flesh could not.

pos: adj. (of Italy; in Scripture, the name of the cohort Cornelius commanded)
etymology: From Italy, Latin Italia; used once in Scripture, of the band or cohort at Caesarea which Cornelius commanded.
biblical_def: Italian occurs once in Scripture, and it is the detail that opens the door of the church to the Gentiles. “There was a certain man in Caesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band” (Acts 10:1). The band was a cohort of auxiliaries raised in Italy — Roman soldiers of the occupying power, quartered in a Jewish province. The man who commanded them was not a proselyte of the covenant but he was no idolater either: “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway” (Acts 10:2). An angel told him his devotion had been noticed: “And when he looked on him, he was afraid, and said, What is it, Lord? And he said unto him, Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God” (Acts 10:4) — and sent him to fetch a preacher, for the prayers and the alms had not saved him. What Peter learned in that house broke a wall: “Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). The gospel went first to a Gentile in Roman uniform, and the uniform is named.

corruption_summary: Sincere devotion is treated as sufficient; Cornelius prayed always and gave much alms, and still had to be sent a preacher.
corruption_paragraphs: Cornelius is the standing case against the idea that a sincere and generous religion saves a man without the gospel. He feared God, he prayed always, he gave much alms, and an angel of God testified that his prayers were remembered — and the angel's errand was to send him for Peter, that he might hear words whereby he should be saved. Sincerity brought him the messenger; it did not do the messenger's work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is that God is no respecter of persons, that He saves Gentile soldiers and Jewish fishermen on the same terms, and that He is pleased to send a preacher to a man He has already begun to draw.
